lines.text: If my battery died tonight, this would stay up for weeks. Wrong, but confident.
lines.note: E-ink keeps its last picture with no power. The screen imagines itself frozen on a stale forecast and is proud mostly of the attitude.

lines.text: Every time this line changes, I go black for a second. Nobody asks if I'm okay.
lines.note: The e-ink refresh flash, seen from inside: a little self-pity about the screen's own hourly job.

lines.text: That sentence works all evening. My lines rotate hourly, like lifeguards.
lines.note: Points at the bold sentence, which stays up all evening, against the hourly rotation of the sarcastic line. Lifeguards rotate so nobody gets numb.

lines.text: I go on last, after the drawings and the sentence. Headliners always do.
lines.note: The line's real spot on the screen, at the bottom, recast as top billing. Pure screen vanity, and true to the layout.

lines.text: Some people trust only their porch thermometer. It's been in direct sun since 1994.
lines.note: Other forecasters: the household rival with a homemade data source that always reads high.

lines.text: Checking three apps and believing the nicest isn't forecasting. It's voting.
lines.note: Other people's habit of shopping for the weather they want; the screen names it for what it is.

lines.text: I pick an outfit nightly and never hear how it went. Like having a kid in college.
lines.note: The screen's job has no feedback loop. Parents whose kids never call back know the feeling.

lines.text: The whole town gets this weather, and I drew one person. Budget cuts.
lines.note: The drawing shows one figure for weather that covers everyone; the screen explains the cast size like a cheap production.

lines.text: Newspapers did the weather in black and white for a century. Mine doesn't rub off.
lines.note: The screen as heir to the newspaper weather box, with one upgrade: e-ink doesn't come off on anyone's hands.

lines.text: The weather has no idea what day it is. I put it on the tag anyway, for morale.
lines.note: Reacts to the day in the black tag ('Tomorrow · Sat'). Weather doesn't care; the screen labels it for the humans.

lines.text: People will describe this weather to each other while standing right in it.
lines.note: Other people's habit: weather small talk delivered to someone who is in the same weather.

lines.text: Swedes say there's no bad weather, only wrong clothes. So it's all on me.
lines.note: Takes a famous saying literally: if clothes are the only variable, the outfit screen is responsible for everything. Self-importance as a punch.

lines.text: I'm a paper doll with internet. Somehow that makes me a smart device.
lines.note: What the screen really does (dress one flat figure every night), followed by its inflated job title.

lines.text: Whatever that sentence says, somebody will call it 'typical.'
lines.note: Points at the bold sentence: there's always someone who calls any weather typical. Works under every forecast.

lines.text: It says 'Fri' up there. For most people, that's the whole forecast.
lines.note: Points at the day in the black tag. On a Friday night the weekday is the only news people take in.

lines.text: Some people still forecast by looking out a window the night before. Bold method.
lines.note: Other forecasters: the amateur who checks the window in the evening for tomorrow's weather. Dry respect for a method that can't work.

lines.text: Stylists charge thousands per outfit. I work for the occasional recharge.
lines.note: The screen's job against the professionals' rate; TRMNL runs on a battery that needs charging now and then.
